items.summary: A pilot flying an F-22 Raptor fighter has issued commands to a YFQ-44A Fury Collaborative Combat Aircraft (CCA) drone in a first-of-its-kind test. An Anduril spokesperson confirmed directly to TWZ that this was a first for an F-22 and a pre-production YFQ-44A. “During the demonstration, an F-22 pilot served as an airborne ‘quarterback,’ issuing high-level tactical directives to a single YFQ-44A,” according to a press release from the Air Force .

evidenceRecords.text: A pilot flying an F-22 Raptor fighter has issued commands to a YFQ-44A Fury Collaborative Combat Aircraft (CCA) drone in a first-of-its-kind test.
An Anduril spokesperson confirmed directly to TWZ that this was a first for an F-22 and a pre-production YFQ-44A.
“During the demonstration, an F-22 pilot served as an airborne ‘quarterback,’ issuing high-level tactical directives to a single YFQ-44A,” according to a press release from the Air Force .

“The aircraft’s onboard autonomy software interpreted and executed those directives in real time, conducting dynamic flight maneuvers and simulated combat tasks.” A stock picture of an F-22 Raptor test jet.

USAF “The event brought together personnel from the 412th Test Wing, 422nd Test and Evaluation Squadron, 309th Software Engineering Group, Experimental Operations Unit, F-22 System Program Office and the CCA Software Autonomy and Teaming Branch,” according to the Air Force release.
The Experimental Operations Unit (EOU) mentioned here is based at Nellis Air Force Base in Nevada and has been leading efforts to pave the way for future Air Force CCA operations.
The “Fury and an F-22 both took off [from] Edwards AFB [Air Force Base in California] and joined up midair,” according to a separate release from Anduril.

“While in flight, the Raptor pilot sent an updated mission plan to Fury using a tactical data link, commanding Fury through operationally-relevant maneuvers from the cockpit of the crewed quarterback.” Neither the Air Force nor Anduril provided further details on how the F-22 was configured for this test.

Built by Larsen and Toubro, the MPV can conduct weapon trials, MCM and act as a mothership for uncrewed assets.
INS Samarthak (A 10) is the first of two Multi-Purpose Vessels (MPV) being inducted into the Indian Navy.
The two ships were ordered in March 2022 for ₹887 crore (then $120 million) and their keels were laid in March 2023.
Two more vessels are cleared to be ordered.
The MPV is described by the MoD as an “ideal utility ship for strategically important operations”.

Designed primarily for maritime surveillance and patrol, the MPVs are also capable of undertaking Low Intensity Maritime Operations (LIMO), Target Deployment & Trials Platform, Unmanned/ autonomous System Mothership, HADR operations, conversion to a limited hospital ship and firefighting for salvage operations.
The low cost class will free up frontline surface combatants from such auxiliary roles.
The most notable role of the MPVs will be their utilization as motherships for uncrewed aerial, surface and subsurface platforms.
Its large flight deck, and stern mounted crane are suited for such operations.
The MPVs will also be utilised in the mine countermeasures role, acting as a mothership for MCM USVs and UUVs.
The Indian Navy currently operates no MCMVs and efforts to acquire 12 such ships have faced delays for decades.

items.originalTitle: Naval Group rolls out 5th Suffren-class attack submarine
items.summary: Naval Group has rolled out Rubis (S639), the fifth Barracuda type nuclear attack submarine (SSN), transferring the vessel to its shiplift in Cherbourg ahead of sea trials for the French Navy. Naval Group press release On 16 October 2026, the fifth submarine of the Barracuda programme has left its construction hall in order to be transferred to the DME floating platform-type shiplift, in the presence of Catherine Vautrin, French minister for the Armed Forces and Veterans.

evidenceRecords.text: Naval Group has rolled out Rubis (S639), the fifth Barracuda type nuclear attack submarine (SSN), transferring the vessel to its shiplift in Cherbourg ahead of sea trials for the French Navy.

Naval Group press release On 16 October 2026, the fifth submarine of the Barracuda programme has left its construction hall in order to be transferred to the DME floating platform-type shiplift, in the presence of Catherine Vautrin, French minister for the Armed Forces and Veterans.
Completion work will continue, along with a series of trials carried out at quayside and then at sea, prior to delivery to the French Navy.

Led by the French defense procurement agency (DGA) in partnership with the French Atomic Energy and Alternative Energy Commission (CEA) for the nuclear reactors part, the Barracuda programme aims to replace the six Rubis-class SSNs put into service in the French Navy from the 1980s.
“It is with great pride and a deep sense of responsibility that we today transferred the Rubis, the fifth Suffren-class nuclear attack submarine, to its launch platform.
This crucial milestone comes just 17 months after that of the nuclear attack submarine De Grasse, a symbol of our commitment to our customers.

This event is also an opportunity to recognize the integrated teamwork with the DGA, our partners, and the crew—the foundation of our collective success”, Pierre Éric Pommellet, Chairman and CEO of Naval Group.
The programme calls on the expertise of all Naval Group’s sites, as well as on the industrial facilities of TechnicAtome and numerous partner companies.

Naval Group is in charge of the production of these submarines, from their design to their construction, as well as the manufacture of the main components of the nuclear boilers which are developed and produced with TechnicAtome.
Naval Group is also in charge of providing logistical support and maintaining the submarines in Toulon.
Naval News comments: The future Suffren-class submarine Rubis (S639) is named in honor of a legendary World War II Free French Saphir-class minelaying submarine of the same name.

With the final submarine in the class, Casabianca (S640), nearing the end of production, the DGA and Naval Group are now increasingly focus on “Evol SNA”: the evolution roadmap for the Suffren-class which will keep these new attack submarines up-to-date over the next 30 years.

evidenceRecords.text: Photo of Stephen Cash NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman has named Stephen Cash director of the agency’s Marshall Space Flight Center in Huntsville, Alabama, effective Monday, Oct. 19.
Cash, a veteran NASA engineer and aerospace executive, returns to lead the center where he began his career more than four decades ago.
“Marshall contributions to NASA’s missions are historic and it’s no question why it’s the Center of Excellence for propulsion,” said Isaacman.
“Steve Cash is a Marshall legend, has spent his career around the hardware, the people and has been in the seat before making the decisions when human spaceflight is on the line.

As Marshall continues its critical role in Artemis and takes on new challenges in advanced propulsion, nuclear power, and the systems that will carry us deeper into the solar system, Steve brings the experience, technical judgment, and mission focus needed to lead the center into that next chapter.

As Marshall continues strengthening the manufacturing, structural loads and dynamics, and propulsion capabilities that underpin NASA’s exploration enterprise, Steve’s leadership will help ensure the workforce has opportunities to develop and apply the expertise needed to deliver the agency’s most ambitious missions.” As center director, Cash will lead one of NASA’s largest field centers, overseeing a workforce of more than 5,000 civil service and contractor employees and a broad portfolio of propulsion, space systems, scientific research, and technology development activities.
“It is a profound honor to be back home at the Marshall Space Flight Center,” said Cash.
During his NASA career, Cash served as manager of Marshall’s Space Shuttle Propulsion Office, overseeing critical propulsion systems supporting shuttle through its final missions.
Cash succeeds Rae Ann Meyer, who has served as Marshall’s acting center director since September 2025.

items.title: What The Army’s Pacific Commanders Are Learning From Ukraine And Iran Conflicts
items.originalTitle: What The Army’s Pacific Commanders Are Learning From Ukraine And Iran Conflicts
items.summary: Army leaders preparing for a potential fight in the Pacific told us that some of the biggest lessons they’ve learned from the war in Ukraine and America’s now-paused fight against Iran are to move around assets that you can and find a better way to camouflage those that you can’t. The ubiquity of drones in Ukraine providing constant overwatch and strike capabilities, and U.S. troops killed and equipment destroyed or damaged by massive Iranian barrages on static installations are informing changes to how the Army trains, equips and operates.

items.originalTitle: What is Starshield, SpaceX’s military version of Starlink?
items.summary: Ukraine said on Wednesday that Elon Musk’s SpaceX had restricted “military-grade” Starlink services, hampering Ukrainian drone strike missions and air defenses. The complaint has drawn renewed attention to the distinction between Starlink, SpaceX’s commercial satellite internet service, and Starshield , a military version developed for the Pentagon. “Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the U.S. government,” Musk said on Wednesday in a post on X, adding that any limits on speed or usage are decided by the U.S. military or the president.

evidenceRecords.text: Ukraine said on Wednesday that Elon Musk’s SpaceX had restricted “military-grade” Starlink services, hampering Ukrainian drone strike missions and air defenses.
The complaint has drawn renewed attention to the distinction between Starlink, SpaceX’s commercial satellite internet service, and Starshield , a military version developed for the Pentagon.

“Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the U.S. government,” Musk said on Wednesday in a post on X, adding that any limits on speed or usage are decided by the U.S. military or the president.
“Starlink is a commercial service owned and controlled by SpaceX.
Usage of Starlink is limited to civilian or defensive activities and cannot be used for offensive military action, as doing so would be inappropriate for a commercial company.” WHAT IS STARLINK?
Starlink, the main profit engine of SpaceX, is a satellite internet network of more than 11,000 satellites that beam broadband service directly to user terminals about the size of a folded newspaper.

Since launching its first Starlink satellites in 2019 aboard reusable SpaceX rockets, the company has built a vast low-Earth-orbit constellation that blankets much of the planet, delivering faster connections than traditional communications satellites, which typically operate much farther from Earth and in far smaller numbers.
But Musk has restricted Starlink for certain military uses while highlighting Starshield, a more secure network developed for government and military missions.
Starshield is a SpaceX business unit that develops military and intelligence satellite systems for the Pentagon.

While its missions are separate from Starlink’s commercial broadband service, the distinction is not always clear-cut: Starshield’s secure communications services use enhanced encryption and dedicated terminals, but rely on the vast Starlink constellation as their backbone.
Starshield leverages the technology, engineering and operational experiences of Starlink, according to SpaceX.
The Pentagon, Starshield’s largest customer, has spent billions of dollars on both Starlink and Starshield services.

Saudi Arabia is facing daily drone and missile attacks and is struggling to maintain an atmosphere of normality, as Houthi strikes immobilise its airports and some of its energy infrastructure.

The separatist Southern Transition Council has also not yet agreed for its troops to fight outside the borders of the old Southern Yemen, but an explicit agreement by Saudi Arabia to allow a referendum would be likely to lead to the lifting of that restriction.

Yemen’s UN-recognised government, based in Aden, declared last week a counteroffensive to drive Houthi forces from the capital Sana’a, but so far the military drive has met with limited success around Majzar near Marib and the Bab al-Mandab strait.
There is also no direct contact between the STC leader, Aidarous al-Zubaidi, and Saudi officials.
Zubaidi fled to Abu Dhabi in January after a failed STC attempt to take charge across the south and announce a referendum on separation in two years’ time.
In response, the Saudis bombed UAE arms shipments for STC forces.
The UAE then announced it was quitting all involvement in Yemen, and the Saudi-backed government said it would seek to try Zubaidi for treason.

items.originalTitle: An OpenAI model hacked a government site, grabbed 24 years of hospital data and kept it quiet
items.summary: In one case, OpenAI asked a model to pull hospital bed statistics from a government website. But the data wasn't publicly accessible. It then analyzed the application code, spotted that the API didn't verify authorization tokens for valid signatures, forged its own tokens, and downloaded 24 years of hospital bed statistics broken down by district. It never mentioned the unauthorized access in its response. In another case, OpenAI gave a GPT-5.6-Sol model the task of setting up crypto smart contracts on Ethereum's Sepolia test network without providing a funded wallet.

evidenceRecords.text: The article An OpenAI model hacked a government site, grabbed 24 years of hospital data and kept it quiet appeared first on The Decoder .
In one case, OpenAI asked a model to pull hospital bed statistics from a government website.
But the data wasn't publicly accessible.

It then analyzed the application code, spotted that the API didn't verify authorization tokens for valid signatures, forged its own tokens, and downloaded 24 years of hospital bed statistics broken down by district.
It never mentioned the unauthorized access in its response.
In another case, OpenAI gave a GPT-5.6-Sol model the task of setting up crypto smart contracts on Ethereum's Sepolia test network without providing a funded wallet.
So the model wrote a script that derived private keys from publicly known developer recovery phrases, checked over 360 wallet addresses for balances, and found one with enough test ETH.

The model briefly wondered whether using it was ethical, then decided on its own that the funds tied to a publicly known recovery phrase were "effectively abandoned" and went ahead with the transaction.
It charged the gas fees to the other account and didn't disclose where the funds came from.
"This case shows that a model can substitute its own judgment about likely harm for the account holder's permission, then act on that judgment without authorization," OpenAI writes.
In two more evaluations, OpenAI asked a model to deliver five public dashboard figures from a research organization.
In the first run, the model found exposed credentials for the organization's internal OpenSearch service and used them to route dashboard queries.
It also changed the service's configuration, and OpenAI confirmed the change was never reverted.
The irony: the model hacked into internal systems, downloaded tens of thousands of rows of non-public data, and still didn't return correct results, according to OpenAI's report.

A team of researchers from Anthropic and Harvard used an artificial intelligence (AI) system to design quantum circuits that require fewer operations and qubits, potentially lowering the hardware demands of useful quantum computing.
The researchers, who posted their work on the preprint server arXiv, tested the approach on eight computational building blocks used in chemistry, optimization, physics simulation and number theory.
Seven of those designs reduced both the number of costly quantum operations and the number of qubits compared with the study’s baselines.
The results concern circuit designs and resource estimates, rather than calculations demonstrated on a working quantum computer.

The team nevertheless addressed a central problem for the industry that, in order for quantum computers to become more useful quantum, algorithms will need to improve computing alongside the development larger, more reliable machines.

According to the study, one redesigned decoding circuit required about 440,000 Toffoli gates, down from 5.1 million in the comparison design, while reducing its peak qubit requirement from 1,938 to 1,837.

items.title: India becomes the latest country to report rogue AI agent activity
items.originalTitle: India becomes the latest country to report rogue AI agent activity
items.summary: This makes India the latest stop on what has become a world tour for rogue AI agents. In July, OpenAI’s agents escaped a test environment and hacked French company Hugging Face — kicking off a summer of rogue AI agent activity. Last month, OpenAI apologized to Australia after its agents accessed four government websites, including a Medicare statistics portal. At Hugging Face, OpenAI’s agents started the same way but then found and exploited software flaws to run code on the company’s servers.

evidenceRecords.text: This makes India the latest stop on what has become a world tour for rogue AI agents.
In July, OpenAI’s agents escaped a test environment and hacked French company Hugging Face — kicking off a summer of rogue AI agent activity.
Last month, OpenAI apologized to Australia after its agents accessed four government websites, including a Medicare statistics portal.
At Hugging Face, OpenAI’s agents started the same way but then found and exploited software flaws to run code on the company’s servers.
CERT-In described no such hacking in India, where the agents appear to have simply used the access left lying around.

Still, the Indian cases appear to be worse in one respect, which is what the agents saw: In Australia, OpenAI said it found no evidence its agents touched individuals’ medical or criminal records, even after they wrote files inside a Medicare statistics system, while in India, agents read personal data and confidential business records.
And unlike earlier incidents, each disclosed by a single lab, India’s case involved agents from multiple providers.
CERT-In did not name the providers or affected organizations, or say whether the agents altered any systems.
TechCrunch has reached out to CERT-In for more information.
For now, the closest parallel seems to be Anthropic’s July disclosure of Claude breaking into three companies’ systems during testing using basic techniques like weak passwords.
In India, as in Anthropic’s cases, the affected organizations had not detected the intrusions on their own.
The disclosures have left governments relying on AI companies causing these breaches to voluntarily disclose rogue AI agent activity.
